A26
A case of Type 1 diabetes with stiff person syndrome
and coeliac disease
LA Behan /C3, EP O’Sullivan /C3, TJF King /C3, O Hardiman w, A Agha /C3,
CJ Thompson /C3and D Smith /C3
/C3Department of Diabetes and Endocrinology, Beaumont Hospital,
Royal College of Surgeons of Ireland, Dublin, Ireland, wDepartment of
Neurology, Beaumont Hospital, Royal College of Surgeons of Ireland,
Dublin, Ireland
Background: Type 1 diabetes is associated with a variety of
autoimmune conditions, including both coeliac disease, and less
commonly stiff person syndrome, a rare neurological condition
characterised by muscle stiffness usually affecting the spine and
lower limbs, characterised by positivity for anti glutamic acid
decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies.
Case report: A 41-year-old man with a 2 year history of coeliac
disease, presented with painful muscular cramps and stiffness in his
back. On examination, there was hypertonicity in both lower
limbs. Random plasma glucose was 36.4 mmol/l, with no ketonaemia
or acidosis. Anti-GAD antibodies were positive at 105 U/ml
(reference range 0–1). Type 1 diabetes and stiff person syndrome
were diagnosed. The patient was treated with plasmapheresis
and intravenous immunoglobulin. This resulted in a reduction
in serum (4 U/ml) and cerebrospinal fluid (61 U/ml) anti-GAD
antibody titres, as well as a marked clinical improvement. The
patient was commenced on basal bolus insulin regimen for his
diabetes.
Conclusions: This, to our knowledge, is the first reported case of
Type 1 diabetes, stiff person syndrome, and coeliac disease occurring
simultaneously. In addition, it highlights the importance of
considering all other autoimmune conditions, however rare, in
patients with Type 1 diabetes presenting with atypical clinical or
biochemical features.
